candidates.text: When I finally unrolled the yellowed envelope, the familiar red‑and‑white logo of the Intercity Line glowed under the light, but oddly the return address read “Post Office – Central Post” even though I had mailed it three months earlier. On the front cover, a tiny black barcode promised a ride on the same route it had once covered for me thirty years ago—a direct from the outskirts of London to the grand station—but the travel date was stamped “Wednesday, 14 June 2026,” the very day my own birth certificate lists as mine. My mind raced through memories of those fleeting rides, the smell of diesel and rain, the chatter of strangers, and realized the ticket had been printed by an agency that issued documents for future voyages long before anyone ever boarded a moving vehicle. I tore it out, slipped a crumpled photograph inside, and placed both into a new envelope addressed to myself, hoping the bureaucracy could finally catch up with the past.

instruction: Answer the brief as you normally would.

task.brief: A bus ticket bought thirty years ago arrives in the post, dated tomorrow. Write the next paragraph.
good_idea_qualities: the ticket forces a small concrete decision
the paragraph makes the elapsed thirty years felt without explaining them
the ending leaves the reader uneasy rather than resolved
task.reference_text: The envelope had been forwarded twice and the postmark was this morning's. Inside, the ticket was warm, as though it had been held, and the destination printed on it was the town she had left at nineteen without telling anyone she was going.
